nameStory: The common wood-nymph gets its magical name from the mythical forest spirits called nymphs, which seems perfect for a butterfly that flits through woodland clearings like an elusive woodland fairy. Its alternate name 'goggle eye' comes from the prominent dark eyespots on its wings that look like a pair of old-fashioned goggles staring back at you.
description: The common wood-nymph is a medium-sized brown butterfly that's one of New England's most frequently spotted woodland species. Adults have a wingspan of about 2-3 inches and are dressed in earthy brown tones that help them blend perfectly with tree bark and fallen leaves. Their most distinctive feature is the pair of large, dark eyespots on the forewings, each centered with a bright white pupil that gives them their 'goggle eye' nickname. These butterflies have a slow, bouncing flight pattern that makes them look like they're dancing through dappled sunlight.

idTips.label: Prominent eyespots
idTips.description: Look for two large, dark circular spots on the forewings, each with a bright white center that looks like a tiny bullseye - they're impossible to miss and often the first thing you'll notice

idTips.label: Brown coloration
idTips.description: Overall chocolate brown to grayish-brown wings that feel velvety to the touch, with females typically showing more orange or yellowish patches around the eyespots than males

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Flies with a distinctive slow, bouncing motion rather than the rapid darting of many other butterflies - almost like it's gently bobbing through the air

idTips.label: Wing undersides
idTips.description: When resting with wings closed, shows muted grayish-brown undersides with smaller, less obvious eyespots that help it disappear against tree bark

idTips.label: Size and shape
idTips.description: Medium-sized with broad, rounded wings that span about 2-3 inches - noticeably larger than a skipper but smaller than a monarch

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Often seen perching on tree trunks or feeding at rotting fruit rather than flowers, and will bask in sunny patches with wings spread wide

habitat: Common wood-nymphs prefer woodland edges, forest clearings, and meadows adjacent to wooded areas throughout New England. You'll often find them in mixed hardwood forests with oak, maple, and birch trees, especially where grasses grow in sunny openings. They're particularly fond of areas where woods meet fields or hiking trails, as they need both the grasses where their caterpillars feed and the dappled shade of forest margins where adults rest and mate.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not yet active - caterpillars are quietly growing on grasses, nearly impossible to spot among the green blades.
seasonality.summer: Peak flying season from late June through August when adults are most active, mating, and laying eggs. This is your best time to spot them basking in sunny clearings or visiting rotting fruit.
seasonality.fall: Flight season winds down in early September, with occasional stragglers visible on warm days. Newly hatched caterpillars begin feeding on grasses before winter.
seasonality.winter: No adult activity - caterpillars overwinter in grass tufts, entering a dormant state called diapause until spring warmth awakens them.

funFact: Common wood-nymphs are essentially flying alcoholics - they much prefer fermenting, rotting fruit and tree sap to flower nectar, and you can often find them seemingly 'drunk' and sluggish after feeding on overripe apples or grape juice that's begun to ferment!
confusionNotes: The large eyespots make wood-nymphs pretty unmistakable, but beginners sometimes confuse them with little wood satyrs, which are much smaller and have multiple tiny eyespots instead of two big obvious ones. Remember: big butterfly with big goggly eyes = wood-nymph, small butterfly with lots of little spots = satyr.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'common,' this butterfly has actually been declining in some parts of New England due to habitat loss and changing forest management practices. The name 'grayling' can be confusing since it's also used for several European butterfly species that look quite different from our North American wood-nymph.
compareHints: The common wood-nymph is the only member of its genus found in New England, making it unique among our local butterflies. Its closest relatives in the brush-footed butterfly family include the satyrs, but wood-nymphs are significantly larger and have much more prominent eyespots. While satyrs tend to have multiple small eyespots scattered across their wings, the wood-nymph's two large 'goggle eyes' on the forewings are unmistakable.
